evaluation.positioning_hook: After her ex-boyfriend is murdered at school, Macy digs into a buried teen death and awakens a black-cloaked killer who turns her grief into a body-count mystery.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The core promise is easy to sell: a popular high-school circle, a murdered ex, and a buried past death that turns the campus into a fear engine. The teen-horror lane is proven, though this version leans more niche than four-quadrant because the emotional entry point is grief and investigation rather than broad wish-fulfillment.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The opening murder, the school assembly, and Macy’s vow to investigate establish the premise clearly. The hook becomes more specific once Lillian Crawford enters the story, but the script still spends a stretch on mood and social setup before the central supernatural engine fully locks in.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Macy has a clean emotional engine — guilt, anger, and determination — and the Outlanders give her a social orbit. The supporting players are more functional than singular, so the character appeal lives primarily in Macy’s grief-to-obsession turn and the actor who can carry that shift.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s boldest move is pairing glossy teen-group dynamics with a murder mystery that quickly tips into slasher territory. The school-assembly death announcement and the later warehouse attack give it a sharper edge than a standard teen whodunit, though the overall framework still sits in familiar genre territory.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The opening death, the assembly reveal, and the research sequence create a steady pull, and the warehouse kill closes the episode with real force. There is some repetition in grief beats and conversation scenes, but the escalation is clear and the final head-in-a-box beat in Episode 2 shows the story knows how to punch.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a socially dominant teen clique being pulled into a murder-and-urban-legend spiral has immediate appeal, and Lillian’s return as a predatory figure gives the premise a memorable image. It feels fresh enough to stand out in the teen-horror shelf, though not yet in the rarefied territory of a truly singular genre signature.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The wealthy suburban school, the Outlanders’ status, and the old school archive create a usable world with social hierarchy and history. Most of the texture is still in service of the plot, so the setting reads as a strong container rather than a fully self-generating ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a recognizable blend of glossy teen banter, melodramatic grief, and sudden violence, and the music cues reinforce that identity. The tone is consistent, but it still sits close to adjacent teen mystery-horror pieces rather than announcing a fully singular voice.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Macy’s guilt over Ryan and the buried history around Lillian suggest a deeper mythology under the surface, and the school’s past deaths hint at a larger pattern. The material clearly wants to open into more, even if the current pages mostly foreground the immediate murder mystery.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Outlanders have a workable group dynamic, with teasing, status, and shared shock giving the ensemble some life. At this stage, though, the relationships mostly orbit Macy and the central mystery rather than generating fully independent story energy.

casting_characteristics: One principal teen lead role with strong emotional range

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interiors with some exterior school, street, courtyard, and warehouse scenes

technical.vfx_details: A few stylized murder beats and the supernatural presentation of Lillian; mostly practical presentation with possible enhancement for speed/appearance.
technical.sfx_needs: Blood effects, body impact beats, tire blowout/crash imagery, severed-head reveal in a box

rights_flags.detail: "Happier Than Ever" by Billie Eilish and "When the Party's Over" by Billie Eilish are specifically named and used as mood cues.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Streaming horror-thriller or teen genre feature lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with strong streamer-friendly genre packaging; the mystery-and-kill escalation supports a festival-to-platform or direct streaming path.

cost.note: Contemporary school, home, and warehouse settings keep the footprint contained, with only modest effects and practical gore.

cast.note: A teen ensemble plus parents, police, and school staff requires a broad but manageable cast, with the Macy role carrying the center of gravity.

location.note: The story moves through school interiors, suburban exteriors, a home, and a warehouse, but the locations are all contemporary and accessible.

content.note: Murder, blood, grief, and a severed-head reveal push the material firmly into mature horror-thriller territory.

rights.note: Two Billie Eilish songs are explicitly named and would need clearance if retained.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The opening murder is immediate and legible.
strengths.what_it_means: The script starts with a clean genre promise: a stylish teen is violently taken out before the audience has time to settle, which is exactly the kind of cold-open that sells a horror feature fast. Teen-horror buyers and streamers looking for a high-concept hook with instant stakes will understand the lane in seconds.
strengths.evidence: Ryan’s limo attack in the opening pages, ending with him thrown into the street and left dying.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Macy is built around grief and guilt.
strengths.what_it_means: That emotional engine gives the lead role real traction beyond the mystery plot, making the movie playable as both a scare piece and a character-forward revenge investigation. Young actresses who want a showcase turn with anger, vulnerability, and obsession in one part will see the opportunity immediately, and buyers know that kind of lead can carry a franchise starter.
strengths.evidence: Macy’s repeated calls to Ryan, her breakdown after the assembly, and her vow not to let his death go.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The school setting has social hierarchy baked in.
strengths.what_it_means: The Outlanders, the wealthy neighborhood, and the school’s status culture give the story a built-in social map that can support both suspense and audience identification. That makes the project attractive to teen-genre buyers who want a recognizable world with enough texture to feel premium rather than generic.
strengths.evidence: The group’s swagger outside the mansion, the whispered attention from other students, and the school’s public assembly.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The assembly reveal lands like a set-piece.
strengths.what_it_means: The public announcement of Ryan’s murder turns private dread into communal shock, which is a strong theatrical-style beat even in a streaming-first market. Producers looking for a contained but eventful midpoint-style jolt will recognize the value of a scene that can be marketed in a trailer.
strengths.evidence: Principal Hawthorne’s announcement in the auditorium, with police present and students reacting in waves.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Lillian gives the story a visual monster.
strengths.what_it_means: The black-cloaked, inhuman version of Lillian creates a memorable face for the threat, which is crucial for horror marketing and poster art. Genre buyers and directors who like a creature-adjacent slasher icon will respond to a villain who can be teased, feared, and instantly recognized.
strengths.evidence: The warehouse attack where Lillian appears as a pale, black-cloaked predator and kills Alex.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending escalates cleanly into a body-count engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The head-in-a-box beat confirms the movie is not just a mystery but a kill-driven horror feature, which broadens the commercial lane into slasher territory. That kind of escalation is attractive to buyers who want a clear promise of more set-pieces and a trailer-friendly final image.
strengths.evidence: Episode 2’s box delivery containing Alex Mercer’s head.

whats_special.headline: This has a clean, marketable teen-horror engine: a popular school clique, a murdered ex, a buried local death, and a returning predator with a face. The strongest asset is Macy, whose grief turns into obsession in a way that can anchor both scares and emotion, while the school setting and Lillian mythology give the project a trailer-ready identity.

lead_characters.name: Macy
lead_characters.hook: Macy is the emotional center of the piece: outwardly polished, socially fluent, and quick with a joke, but internally running on guilt, anger, and the need to make meaning out of loss. She starts as the girl trying to keep her morning bright and ends as the one willing to chase a buried truth into the dark, which gives the role a clean arc from teen confidence to obsessive resolve.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Sophie Nélisse in The Book Thief or Maika Monroe in It Follows — a lead whose stillness and emotional pressure do as much work as the scares. It gives a young actor the chance to play grief, suspicion, and determination in a genre frame, with the kind of central turn that can define a breakout performance.

lead_characters.name: Jessica
lead_characters.hook: Jessica is the polished social glue of the group, stylish and confident on the surface, but she softens fast when the murder hits home. She functions as the friend who can keep the room moving until the room stops moving, which makes her useful as both comic rhythm and emotional witness.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of best-friend role that gave Auliʻi Cravalho in Mean Girls or Beanie Feldstein in Booksmart a chance to balance wit with vulnerability. It offers a young actor a high-visibility ensemble part with sharp reactions, group chemistry, and a few key emotional beats.

lead_characters.name: Kyle
lead_characters.hook: Kyle is the smug, effortless alpha of the group, the one who jokes first and processes later, until the murder strips away the performance. He reads as a status kid with enough charm to lead a room, which makes his shock and guilt more playable when the story turns darker.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This sits in the lane of the privileged teen roles that let actors like Jacob Elordi in Euphoria or Austin Abrams in The Walking Dead play charisma with a crack in it. It gives a young actor a chance to weaponize charm, then let the mask slip under pressure.

lead_characters.name: Nina
lead_characters.hook: Nina is the sharp-tongued skeptic, the one who keeps the group honest with sarcasm until fear makes her quieter. She has the best built-in edge in the ensemble, because she can pivot from comic bite to genuine unease without changing her basic rhythm.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of dry, fast-talking supporting part that gave Alexa Demie in Euphoria or Ayo Edebiri in The Bear early scene-stealing space. It gives an actor a chance to land jokes, then turn the same voice into dread when the mystery stops being theoretical.

lead_characters.name: Ethan
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the group’s jokester, the one who uses humor as social glue until the murders make the jokes land differently. He’s the easiest character to underestimate, which gives him room to become unexpectedly useful as the story darkens.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of comic-relief-with-shadows part that gave Justice Smith in The Get Down or Noah Centineo in To All the Boys a chance to shift from charm to sincerity. It offers a young actor a visible ensemble slot with room for timing, warmth, and a late-breaking emotional turn.

lead_characters.name: Gabby
lead_characters.hook: Gabby is the younger sibling who still speaks with kid logic, which makes him both disarming and useful as a pressure point in Macy’s home life. He brings innocence into a story that keeps getting darker, and that contrast gives the family scenes a cleaner emotional edge.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of younger-sibling role that gives a child actor a memorable foothold in a genre piece, similar to the grounded kid energy in The Babadook or IT. It offers a small but vivid part that can make a scene land by being the one person in the room who doesn’t yet understand the horror.

lead_characters.name: Mom
lead_characters.hook: Mom is the steady domestic presence, warm and attentive, the person trying to keep the house normal while Macy’s world tilts. She gives the story a grounded family counterweight, which helps Macy’s isolation feel more earned when she pulls away.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded parent role that gave Toni Collette in Hereditary or Connie Britton in The Last House on the Left a chance to anchor the home front before the genre takes over. It offers an actor a contained but emotionally legible part that can deepen the movie’s human stakes.

lead_characters.name: Dad
lead_characters.hook: Dad is the calm, practical parent, present in the margins as the family’s everyday stability. He’s not written as a heavy emotional engine, but he helps establish the normal world that the murder story disrupts.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the sort of understated father role that lets an actor like Kyle Chandler in a family thriller or Mark Ruffalo in a domestic drama bring quiet authority to a few scenes. It gives a performer a clean, efficient support role in a genre feature with real audience visibility.

lead_characters.name: Principal Hawthorne
lead_characters.hook: Principal Hawthorne is the institutional face of the school, formal and strained when he has to deliver the worst possible news to a room full of teenagers. He functions as the voice of authority and containment, which makes the assembly scene feel public and irreversible.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of authority figure role that gives actors in the J.K. Simmons or Jeffrey Wright lane a chance to command a room with very little screen time. It offers a prestige-adjacent supporting part that can land hard in one major scene.

lead_characters.name: Lillian Crawford
lead_characters.hook: Lillian is the story’s buried legend turned active threat: a dead girl whose name carries rumor, history, and fear, and whose return is framed as something feral and predatory. She’s less a conversational character than a mythic presence, which gives the movie its horror iconography.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a performance like Anya Taylor-Joy in The Witch or Samara Weaving in Ready or Not — a role where the actor can be both beautiful and terrifying, human and monstrous. It gives a performer a signature genre part with strong visual branding and the chance to become the face of the film’s menace.

lead_characters.name: Ryan Mitchell
lead_characters.hook: Ryan is the absent center of the story: the ex-boyfriend whose death detonates the plot and whose memory keeps pulling Macy forward. Even though he’s gone early, he matters as the emotional trigger and the first mystery the audience wants solved.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of short-but-crucial role that gave actors in Scream or I Know What You Did Last Summer a chance to make a strong first impression before the story pivots. It offers a young actor a high-impact opening part with a memorable death scene and immediate narrative importance.

lead_characters.name: Alex Mercer
lead_characters.hook: Alex is the curious investigator who pushes the story into its next phase, the one willing to chase the lead into the warehouse and pay for it. He functions as the audience’s proxy for curiosity and danger, which makes his death a clean escalation beat.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of doomed-investigator role that gives an actor a compact but vivid horror showcase, similar to the early victims who briefly steer the story in Final Destination or Fear Street. It offers a punchy part with tension, movement, and a memorable kill sequence.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make teen grief feel dangerous, not sentimental.
director_appeal.fit_profile: First- or second-feature directors, or TV genre directors moving into features, who already work in suspense, horror, or elevated teen drama. The material rewards someone who likes clean set-piece construction, emotional close-ups, and a polished suburban surface that can crack open into violence.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a chance to stage a public-school shock scene, a contained warehouse kill, and a final escalation beat without needing a giant effects canvas. It will attract filmmakers who want to build tension through performance and atmosphere, then punctuate it with a few sharp, trailer-ready horror images.

buyer_appeal.detail: The Macy role can be cast with a rising young lead rather than a name star, while the rest of the ensemble is compact and age-specific. The contemporary school setting, modest effects load, and clear kill-driven hook fit the current streamer appetite for contained genre features that can travel well internationally.

considerations.area: The opening stretch spends time on social texture before the engine locks.
considerations.detail: The limo attack, Macy’s morning routine, and the Outlanders’ walk to school all establish mood and status before the murder mystery fully takes over. A next pass could consider trimming or compressing one of those early beats so the Ryan death and Macy’s investigation arrive with even more forward charge.

The Outlanders have chemistry, but their scenes largely function as reaction space around Macy’s grief and the central mystery. One direction would be to give one supporting friend a more independent pressure point so the group generates more story on its own.

considerations.area: The Billie Eilish cues are doing real mood work.
considerations.detail: Because the script names "Happier Than Ever" and "When the Party’s Over" specifically, those moments carry both tone and clearance implications. If the songs stay, they should be treated as intentional needle drops; if not, the same emotional function can be preserved with original or library music.

considerations.area: The warehouse and school locations keep the footprint contained.
considerations.detail: The story already lives in a manageable set of contemporary spaces, so the cleanest production version is to protect that containment rather than expand the geography. The school, home, courtyard, and warehouse can likely be consolidated further without changing the core mystery engine.
